newsitem.title: USA: Archer Daniels Midland puts another Andreas at helm.
newsitem.headline: Archer Daniels Midland puts another Andreas at helm.

text.p: Agribusiness giant Archer Daniels Midland Co., under fire in recent years for its closed leadership, Thursday named the nephew of long-time leader Dwayne Andreas to replace him as Chief Executive Officer.
Andreas's nephew, Allen Andreas, 53, was named to the CEO post, the agribusiness giant said.

While Dwayne Andreas, 79, is letting go of the day-to-day operations, he remains chairman of the board, which drew some criticism from institutional shareholders who have tried to lessen the executive's influence on the board.
Institutional shareholders, critical of the board of directors, sought greater separation between ADM's management and the board, which had been dominated by friends and relatives of Dwayne Andreas.
The California Public Employees' Retirement System, which holds about 3.6 million ADM shares, called the executive change "a nice step," but continued to call for an independent board at ADM.
"We will continue to ride herd on that company to try to insist that the board of directors be independent," said Patricia Macht, chief of public affairs for Calpers.
Macht said Calpers objects to Dwayne Andreas sitting as chairman, "holding his nephew accountable as chief executive officer."
Jon Lukomnik, New York City's deputy controller, said Allen Andreas had been tapped by ADM as a liasion with institutional shareholders.
"There are concerns, but also opportunities, and I suspect that Allen Andreas will have a shorter honeymoon period (as CEO) than if his last name were not Andreas," Lukomnik said.
"But Allen is smart and a new generation. I think people will be watching closely to see if there is evidence of a corporate culture change."
New York City pensions hold about 3.1 million ADM shares.

Dwayne Andreas' son, Michael, who previously had been considered to be the heir apparent to the top job, has been indicted on antitrust charges. Michael Andreas has pleaded not guilty to those charges.

Decatur, Ill.-based ADM said the executive change comes two months after Dwayne Andreas asked the board's salary, succession and stock option committee to begin implementing a plan of succession by dividing the offices of chairman and chief executive officer.
ADM said the succession committee spent several weeks considering potential candidates for the chief executive post from both inside and outside the company.
Piper Jaffray analyst George Dahlman said that, among the potential inside candidates for the chief executive post, he considered Allen Andreas the top choice.

Allen Andreas, who will be 54 in June, became an attorney in ADM's legal department in 1973. In October 1996, he was named to a four-member office of the chief executive, which also included Dwayne Andreas, President James Randall and Charles Bayless, president of the processing division.
Commenting on the executive changes, Dain Bosworth analyst Bonnie Wittenburg said, "I think the real question is, 'Who becomes chairman?'"
ADM did not indicate how long Dwayne Andreas will remain chairman.
ADM board member Webb said Dwayne Andreas has given his "full support in charging our new CEO to develop a comprehensive succession plan to present to the board."
Prudential Securities analyst John McMillin said that, in a recent conference call, Dwayne Andreas gave no indication that he was stepping down.

"I think the list of positives for Dwayne Andreas is longer than the list of negatives," McMillin said. "He has provided this company with a vision that will last for another 30 years ... using corn starch to make more products."
In other moves, ADM said that Lowell Andreas, a past president of the company and Dwayne Andreas' brother, is retiring from the board.
The company also said Andrew Young, former ambassador to the United Nations, was elected to the board for the balance of the current term.
ADM's stock rose 12.5 cents to $17.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
